score_notes.novelty: Symbol() identity vs Symbol.for() registry as the literal mechanism for Benjamin's aura is a fresh found-object (a language primitive) paired with a mechanism the catalogue lacks; only the web/JS could do it.
score_notes.nuance: Concept and execution collapse cleanly: the === operator is the test of authenticity and fails by design; the description string is the print, the Symbol is the aura, and the console attestation adds a third register without explaining the surface gag.
score_notes.narrative: Names Benjamin directly, stages Duchamp's R. Mutt signature and Ben Vautier's Fluxus gesture, and sits legibly on the chance/order axis (random stroke, ordered baseline); it answers the catalogue's recurring value/authenticity thread with a precise new move.
score_notes.craft: Single self-contained HTML file, no unused code, no fallbacks apologising; the build is the smallest that completes the thought and the ledger/console attestation are load-bearing rather than decorative.
score_notes.wit: The gag lands on the surface (you copied it perfectly and it's still a fake) and again on re-reading as a precise staging of aura; the Symbol.for() button adds a second beat that earns its keep.

references_named: Ben Vautier, Je signe / Tout est art (Fluxus)
Walter Benjamin, The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction (1935)
Marcel Duchamp, R. Mutt signature on Fountain (1917)
rationale: Je signe (===) uses JavaScript's Symbol() identity primitive as the literal mechanism for Benjamin's aura: the description string reproduces perfectly while reference-identity cannot, so forgery === original is always false by design. The mechanism enacts the idea (P1), the work is web-native and perishable (P4), and the chance/order axis is legible in the random stroke over an ordered baseline (P5). It answers the catalogue's recurring value/authenticity thread with a precise new move, double-codes cleanly, and ships as a single self-contained file with CC licence and no tracking.
reservations: The Ben Vautier reference is named but not deeply enacted beyond the title; the Symbol.for() beat is a nice second punch but the work leans heavily on a single JS primitive, which slightly compresses the conceptual surface.
revision_suggestion: Consider a small visual or interactive nod to Vautier's actual gesture (e.g. signing an arbitrary object on the page) so the Fluxus lineage is enacted rather than only cited, and perhaps a third button that exposes the registry collision (two tabs producing the same Symbol.for key) to widen the chance/order staging.
